idiom_name: class/case-class composition + scala.util.Using (Manager for several parts)
implementation_notes: Scala composes with classes and case classes whose constructor parameters are the parts; because case classes are immutable values, a whole with value parts is copied rather than aliased and ownership is trivially safe, while a whole that owns resources must implement AutoCloseable and release them explicitly. scala.util.Using is the library support for that: Using.resource releases even when the body throws (rethrowing the failure), Using.Manager acquires several resources and releases them in reverse order - including when construction of a later part fails - and an implicit Releasable adapts every AutoCloseable, so resource-owning parts participate without extra code. JVM finalization is a dead end (finalize is deprecated for removal), so a Cleaner is only a backstop. The classic Whole/Part structure is unnecessary for immutable data and earns its keep when the whole enforces invariants across mutable parts.
pitfalls: Using scopes the whole, not the parts: handing a part out of the block leaves a client holding a closed part; keep parts inside the whole or hand out copies.
case class equality is structural - two wholes with equal parts compare and hash equal, which is wrong for an owner with identity: use a plain class for stateful wholes.
Mutable parts inside an immutable case class are shared by every copy() of the whole, so both 'owners' mutate one part.
